subs.q: If a word ends in 'sh' or 'ch', like box or church, we add 'es' to the end. How would you spell more than one bus?
subs.h: Write 'bus' and then add 'es'.

Year 1.mastery_q: Look at this sentence: "The two dog run to the house." One word is missing a letter because there are two dogs. Which word is it, and how do you spell it?
Year 1.mastery_hint: Look at the word after "two." It needs a letter at the end to show there is more than one.

Year 1.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Recalling facts, (B) Predicting from pictures/text, (C) Identifying character feelings.

subs.q: Listen to this: "The sun was out and the birds were singing. Sam put on his sun hat." What was the weather like?
subs.h: Was it rainy or was there a hot sun?

subs.q: Sam is wearing a sun hat and carrying a spade. Where do you think he is going?
subs.h: Think of a place with lots of sand.

subs.q: Sam’s ice cream fell on the sand. He started to cry. How is Sam feeling?
subs.h: Is he happy or sad?

Year 1.mastery_q: If the story says "Sam's face turned red and he stomped his feet because he couldn't go to the beach," how is Sam feeling, and why?
Year 1.mastery_hint: Stomping feet usually means someone is ___. Why did the story say he was doing that?

Year 2.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Questions, (B) Identifying Exclamations, (C) Identifying Statements.

subs.q: A Question is a type of sentence that asks something and needs an answer. Which of these is a Question? Options: A) The dog is brown. B) Where is the dog? C) Look at the dog!
subs.h: Look for the sentence that ends with a question mark (?).

subs.q: An Exclamation is a sentence that shows a strong feeling (like being very surprised or excited) and usually starts with 'What' or 'How'. Which of these is an Exclamation? Options: A) What a big dog that is! B) Is that a big dog? C) The dog is big.
subs.h: Look for the sentence that ends with an exclamation mark (!).

subs.q: A Statement is a sentence that tells you a fact or an idea. Which of these is a Statement? Options: A) Pick up the dog. B) How does the dog run? C) The dog is running.
subs.h: This sentence just tells you information and ends with a full stop (.).

Year 2.mastery_q: Read this sentence: "How kind you are to help me!" What type of sentence is this? Options: A) Statement B) Question C) Exclamation D) Command
Year 2.mastery_hint: Does it ask something, tell a fact, or show a strong feeling starting with 'How'?

Year 2.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Meaning of suffix '-ful', (B) Meaning of suffix '-less', (C) Applying suffixes to root words.

subs.q: A Suffix is a group of letters added to the end of a word to change its meaning. The suffix '-ful' means "full of." What does the word "cheerful" mean? Options: A) No cheer B) Full of cheer C) To cheer again
subs.h: Use the definition of '-ful' provided in the question.

subs.q: The suffix '-less' means "without" or "none." What does the word "fearless" mean? Options: A) Full of fear B) Scared C) Without fear
subs.h: Use the definition of '-less' provided in the question.

subs.q: If you take the word "help" and add the suffix that means "without," what is the new word?
subs.h: Put "help" and "-less" together into one word.

Year 2.mastery_q: Fill in the blank with the correct word: "The kitten was very small and could not do anything for itself; it was totally _______."
Year 2.mastery_hint: Choose between "helpful" (full of help) or "helpless" (without help).

Year 2.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Understanding "possession" (belonging), (B) Identifying the apostrophe symbol, (C) Placing the apostrophe for singular nouns.

subs.q: Possession means that something belongs to someone. In the phrase "The hat of the boy," who does the hat belong to? Options: A) The hat B) The boy
subs.h: Who is the person owning the object?

subs.q: We use a symbol called an Apostrophe (') to show belonging. Which of these shows the Apostrophe? Options: A) , B) . C) ' D) !
subs.h: It looks like a comma but sits high up in the air.

subs.q: To show that one girl owns a book, we add 's to her name. Which is correct? Options: A) The girls book B) The girl's book C) The girl s' book
subs.h: The apostrophe must go before the 's' when one person owns something.

Year 2.mastery_q: Rewrite this phrase using an apostrophe to show belonging: "The bone belonging to the dog."
Year 2.mastery_hint: Write the word "dog," add the apostrophe, then add the 's', and finally the word "bone."

Year 2.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying 'because' for reasons, (B) Identifying 'when' for time, (C) Identifying 'if' for conditions.

subs.q: We use the word "because" to give a reason. Complete this: "I ate an apple _______ I was hungry."
subs.h: Why did the person eat the apple? Use the "reason" word.

subs.q: We use the word "when" to talk about a time. Complete this: "I will go outside _______ it stops raining."
subs.h: Use the word that tells us "at what time" the person can go out.

subs.q: We use the word "if" to show that one thing must happen for another thing to happen. Complete this: "You can have a sweet _______ you eat your carrots."
subs.h: This is a choice or a rule. Use the "condition" word.

Year 2.mastery_q: Which word (conjunction) best joins these two ideas: "It was very dark outside ___ the sun had gone down." Options: A) if B) because C) but D) when
Year 2.mastery_hint: Is the second part of the sentence a "reason" why it is dark?

Year 2.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Fact recall, (B) Understanding "Clues" (Inference), (C) Predicting outcomes.

subs.q: Listen to this: "Molly saw big grey clouds in the sky. She went to the cupboard and grabbed her umbrella." What did Molly see in the sky?
subs.h: Look at the very first sentence.

subs.q: An Inference is when we use "clues" in a story to guess something that isn't written down. If Molly grabbed an umbrella, what does she think is about to happen? Options: A) It will be sunny. B) It will rain. C) It is bedtime.
subs.h: Why do people use umbrellas?

subs.q: Molly's dog was hiding under the sofa and shaking. How is the dog feeling?
subs.h: Does the dog feel happy or scared?

Year 2.mastery_q: Based on the clues (grey clouds, umbrella, shaking dog), what is the most likely thing happening in the story? Options: A) A birthday party B) A thunderstorm C) A trip to the park
Year 2.mastery_hint: Think about what kind of weather has dark clouds, makes you need an umbrella, and might scare a dog with loud noises.

Year 3.section_title: Question Set 1: Transcription (Prefixes - anti, auto, super)
Year 3.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Meaning of 'anti-' (against), (B) Meaning of 'auto-' (self), (C) Meaning of 'super-' (above/beyond).

subs.q: A prefix is a group of letters added to the start of a word to change its meaning. The prefix "anti-" means "against" or "opposite." What does the word "antisocial" mean? Options: A) Very social B) Against being social C) Social by yourself
subs.h: Use the definition of "anti-" provided: it means "against."

subs.q: The prefix "auto-" means "self" or "by itself." What does an "autobiography" mean? Options: A) A book written by someone else B) A book you write about yourself C) A book about cars
subs.h: Use the definition of "auto-" provided: it means "self."

subs.q: The prefix "super-" means "above," "beyond," or "greater than." What is a "supermarket"? Options: A) A small shop B) A market that is larger/greater than a normal shop C) A market that is closed
subs.h: Use the definition of "super-" provided: it means "greater than."

Year 3.mastery_q: Liquid that is used against things freezing is called __________.
Year 3.mastery_hint: Combine the prefix meaning "against" with the word "freeze" to make one word.

Year 3.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying spoken words, (B) Using Inverted Commas, (C) Correct punctuation inside speech.

subs.q: In the sentence: The boy yelled, "Wait for me!" which three words did the boy actually say out loud?
subs.h: Look for the words that come after the comma.

subs.q: We use Inverted Commas (" ") to go around the words someone says. Where should the inverted commas go in this sentence: Help! shouted the girl. Options: A) "Help!" shouted the girl. B) Help! "shouted the girl." C) "Help! shouted" the girl.
subs.h: Put the marks only around the word the girl shouted.

subs.q: When we finish the spoken words, we usually put a comma, exclamation mark, or question mark inside the inverted commas. Which is correct? Options: A) "Go away"! B) "Go away!"
subs.h: The punctuation belongs to the words being said, so it stays inside the " ".

Year 3.mastery_q: Which of these sentences is punctuated correctly for direct speech? Options: A) "Can I have an apple," asked Tom. B) "Can I have an apple?" asked Tom. C) Can I have an apple? "asked Tom."
Year 3.mastery_hint: Tom is asking a question. Does the question mark go inside the speech marks?

Year 3.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying helper verbs (has/have), (B) Distinguishing past tense from present perfect, (C) Using 'has' vs. 'have'.

subs.q: The Present Perfect Tense describes something that happened in the past but is still important now. It uses a "helper verb." Which of these is a helper verb used in this tense? Options: A) played B) has C) jump
subs.h: It is a form of the verb "to have."

subs.q: Which sentence is in the Simple Past Tense?. Options: A) I have eaten my lunch. B) I ate my lunch.
subs.h: The simple past is usually just one action word (verb), without "has" or "have."

subs.q: Which is correct? Options: A) They has gone to the park. B) They have gone to the park.
subs.h: "They" is more than one person, so use "have."

Year 3.mastery_q: Which sentence uses the Present Perfect Tense correctly? Options: A) She has finished her homework. B) She have finished her homework. C) She finished her homework.
Year 3.mastery_hint: You need the helper verb "has" (because it is one girl) + the past version of the action word.

Year 3.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying the topic of a paragraph, (B) Using a dictionary, (C) Summarising across paragraphs.

subs.q: A Paragraph is a group of sentences about the same topic. Read this: "The moon is very dry and dusty. It has no air or water, and nothing can grow there." What is the main topic of this paragraph? Options: A) How to fly to the moon B) What the moon is like C) The history of the moon
subs.h: Is the paragraph telling you what the moon is made of, or how to get there?

subs.q: To find the meaning of a word you don't know, which book should you use?
subs.h: It is an A-Z book of word meanings.

subs.q: An Inference is a conclusion you reach using clues. Read this: "The dog saw the postman. He began to wag his tail and barked happily." How does the dog feel about the postman? Options: A) Angry B) Friendly C) Scared
subs.h: Look for the word "happily" and the action "wag his tail."

Year 3.mastery_q: Read these two paragraphs: What is the main idea of both paragraphs together? Options: A) Why whales live in the ocean. B) Facts about how whales live and breathe. C) How whales catch fish to eat.
Year 3.mastery_hint: Look for a choice that talks about both the ocean (Paragraph 1) and breathing (Paragraph 2).

Year 3.section_title: Question Set 5: Vocabulary (Conjunctions of Time and Cause)
Year 3.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Using 'when' (time), (B) Using 'because' (cause), (C) Using 'before' (sequence).

subs.q: A Conjunction is a joining word. Which conjunction tells us why something happened: "when" or "because"?
subs.h: "I wore a coat ___ it was cold."

subs.q: Which conjunction tells us the time something happened: "if" or "when"?
subs.h: "I will play ___ I finish my work."

subs.q: Which sentence shows the correct order of events? Options: A) Wash your hands before you eat. B) Wash your hands after you eat.
subs.h: When is it most important to have clean hands to stay healthy?

Year 3.mastery_q: Which word best joins these two ideas: "The team celebrated ___ they had won the big game." Options: A) before B) because C) if D) when
Year 3.mastery_hint: Is winning the game the reason (cause) why they are celebrating?

Year 4.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying adverbs of time/place, (B) Identifying the front of a sentence, (C) Using commas after fronted adverbials.

subs.q: An Adverbial is a word or phrase that tells us when, where, or how something happens. Which of these tells us when? Options: A) Under the bridge B) Slowly C) Yesterday morning D) Near the park
subs.h: Which one answers the question "At what time did it happen?"

subs.q: A Fronted Adverbial is when an adverbial is moved to the very start of a sentence. Look at this sentence: "The bell rang at seven o'clock." How would you write that sentence so the time comes first?
subs.h: Start the sentence with "At seven o'clock..."

subs.q: When we use a Fronted Adverbial, we must put a comma after it. Which sentence is punctuated correctly? Options: A) Quietly, the cat crept. B) Quietly the, cat crept. C) Quietly the cat, crept. D) Quietly the cat crept,
subs.h: The comma goes immediately after the "how/when/where" part at the start.

Year 4.mastery_q: Which sentence uses a Fronted Adverbial of place (where) and is punctuated correctly? Options: A) In the dark forest the owls hooted. B) Tomorrow, we will go to the forest. C) Deep inside the cave, a bear slept. D) Running quickly, the boy reached the cave.
Year 4.mastery_hint: Look for a sentence that starts by telling you where something is, followed by a comma.

Year 4.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Singular possession, (B) Identifying plural nouns ending in 's', (C) Placing the apostrophe after the 's' for plurals.

subs.q: Singular Possession is when one person owns something. To show one boy owns a ball, we write: the boy's ball. How do you write that one dog owns a tail?
subs.h: Write 'dog', then an apostrophe ('), then 's'.

subs.q: A Plural noun means more than one. Which of these is the plural of "teacher"? Options: A) teachers B) teacher's C) teachers's D) teacher
subs.h: Most plurals just add 's' at the end with no marks.

subs.q: To show that a group (plural) owns something, we put the apostrophe after the 's'. Which is correct for a group of teachers owning a room? Options: A) the teacher's room B) the teachers' room C) the teachers room'
subs.h: Write the plural "teachers" first, then add the ' at the very end.

Year 4.mastery_q: Rewrite this phrase using a plural possessive apostrophe: "The playground belonging to the boys." (Note: there is more than one boy).
Year 4.mastery_hint: Write the plural word "boys" first. Because it ends in 's', just put the apostrophe (') after the 's'.

Year 4.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying nouns, (B) Defining pronouns, (C) Replacing nouns to avoid repetition.

subs.q: A Noun is a naming word for a person, place, or thing. What is the noun in this sentence: "The bicycle is blue."?
subs.h: Which word is the "thing"?

subs.q: A Pronoun is a word used to replace a noun so we don't repeat it. Which of these is a pronoun? Options: A) Table B) Jump C) He D) Red
subs.h: Which word can you use instead of saying a boy's name?

subs.q: Replace the second "Sarah" with a pronoun: "Sarah ran fast because Sarah was late."
subs.h: Use the word "she."

Year 4.mastery_q: Look at these two sentences: "The children played with the ball. The children threw the ball to the dog." Replace the repeated words in the second sentence with the pronouns "They" and "it".
Year 4.mastery_hint: Rewrite the second sentence starting with "They..." and replacing "the ball" with "it."

Year 4.section_title: Question Set 4: Reading (Word Meaning and Context)
Year 4.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Using a dictionary, (B) Identifying root words, (C) Using context clues.

subs.q: If you are looking for the word "Curious" in a dictionary, which letter of the alphabet should you look under first?
subs.h: Dictionaries are in alphabetical (A-B-C) order.

subs.q: A Root Word is the basic word before a prefix or suffix is added. What is the root word of "unhappiness"?
subs.h: Strip away the "un-" and the "-ness."

subs.q: Read this: "The hiker felt fatigued after walking for ten hours without a break." Based on the sentence, what does fatigued mean? Options: A) Happy B) Very tired C) Hungry D) Fast
subs.h: Think about how you would feel after walking for ten hours.

Year 4.mastery_q: In this sentence, the word "vibrant" describes a garden: "The garden was vibrant, filled with bright red roses, glowing yellow sunflowers, and deep purple lavender." Based on the details about the colors, what is the meaning of the word vibrant?
Year 4.mastery_hint: Does "vibrant" mean dull and grey, or full of bright and exciting colors?

Year 4.section_title: Question Set 5: Vocabulary (Standard English - Verb Agreements)
Year 4.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Singular vs Plural subjects, (B) Correct use of "was" and "were", (C) Identifying non-standard English.

subs.q: In Standard English, we use "was" for one person/thing. Which is correct? Options: A) I was happy. B) I were happy.
subs.h: "I" is one person.

subs.q: We use "were" for more than one person/thing. Which is correct? Options: A) They was playing. B) They were playing.
subs.h: "They" means a group.

subs.q: We also use "did" instead of "done" when there is no helper verb. Which is correct? Options: A) I done my work. B) I did my work.
subs.h: "I done" is non-standard; "I did" is Standard English.

Year 4.mastery_q: Which of these sentences is written in correct Standard English? Options: A) We was going to the shop. B) He done his homework early. C) The birds were singing in the trees. D) They has gone outside.
Year 4.mastery_hint: Check if the subject (one or many) matches the verb ("was" or "were").

Year 5.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Relative Pronouns, (B) Identifying the noun being described, (C) Understanding how to add extra information.

subs.q: A Relative Pronoun is a word like who, which, where, when, whose, or that. It is used to start a section of a sentence that gives more information about a person or thing. Which of these is a Relative Pronoun? Options: A) Under, B) Because, C) Which, D) Slowly.
subs.h: Look for the word used to describe a "thing" (e.g., The car ____ is red).

subs.q: In the sentence, "The astronaut, who was very brave, climbed into the rocket," who is the word "who" giving us more information about?
subs.h: Look at the noun (the person) that comes right before the word "who."

subs.q: A Relative Clause is the part of the sentence that adds extra detail using a relative pronoun. Where does the relative clause end in this sentence: "The book that I bought yesterday is on the table."? Options: A) after 'book', B) after 'yesterday', C) after 'table'.
subs.h: The clause is the "extra information" that could be taken out.

Year 5.mastery_q: Look at these two ideas: 1. The mountain is very high. 2. The mountain is covered in snow. Combine them into one sentence by adding a Relative Clause starting with the word "which" after the word "mountain."
Year 5.mastery_hint: Your sentence should start: "The mountain, which..." and then include the extra information from idea 2.

Year 5.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying modal verbs, (B) Understanding degrees of possibility, (C) Selecting the correct verb for certainty.

subs.q: A Modal Verb is a "helper" word used with another verb to show how certain or possible something is. Examples include: can, could, shall, should, will, would, may, might, and must. Which of these is a Modal Verb? Options: A) Running, B) Might, C) Apple, D) Beautiful.
subs.h: Which word helps tell us if something is possible?

subs.q: If a teacher says, "You must finish your work," does that mean you have a choice, or is it a strict rule? Options: A) A choice, B) A strict rule.
subs.h: "Must" shows a very high level of certainty or obligation.

subs.q: Which word shows that something is less likely to happen? Options: A) Will, B) Might, C) Must.
subs.h: "Will" is a promise; "Might" is just a "maybe."

Year 5.mastery_q: Change the modal verb in this sentence to make the trip sound certain (100% going to happen) instead of just possible: "We might go to the museum tomorrow."
Year 5.mastery_hint: Replace "might" with a word from Sub-Question 1 that shows it will definitely happen.

Year 5.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying extra information, (B) Identifying punctuation for parenthesis, (C) Placing brackets correctly.

subs.q: Parenthesis is extra information added to a sentence. If you remove it, the sentence still makes sense. In this sentence, what is the extra information? "The dog (a large husky) barked loudly."
subs.h: Look at the words inside the curved marks.

subs.q: We can use Brackets ( ), Dashes ( — ), or Commas ( , ) to show parenthesis. Which of these is a pair of Brackets? Options: A) " ", B) ( ), C) ? ?, D) ! !.
subs.h: They look like two curved moons facing each other.

subs.q: Where should the first bracket go in this sentence to show that "who was 10" is extra information? Ben who was 10 won the race.
subs.h: Place it immediately before the word "who."

Year 5.mastery_q: Rewrite this sentence using a pair of brackets to show that "the capital of England" is extra information (parenthesis): "London the capital of England is a busy city."
Year 5.mastery_hint: Put the brackets around the words that tell us what London is.

Year 5.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Recalling facts, (B) Understanding character motive, (C) Finding evidence in the text.

subs.q: Read this: "The hiker checked his map for the fifth time, wiped the sweat from his forehead, and looked at the empty water bottle in his hand. The sun was high in the sky and there was no shade." What was in the hiker's hand?
subs.h: Look at the end of the first sentence.

subs.q: An Inference is a conclusion you reach using clues from the story. Why did the hiker wipe sweat from his forehead? Options: A) He was cold, B) He was hot, C) He was sad.
subs.h: The story says the sun was high and there was no shade.

subs.q: Why is the hiker looking at his map so many times? Options: A) He is lost, B) He likes the colors on the map, C) He is finished walking.
subs.h: When people keep checking a map, it's usually because they aren't sure where they are.

Year 5.mastery_q: Based on the text, give two reasons (evidence) why the hiker might be feeling worried.
Year 5.mastery_hint: Look for clues about his water and his location.

Year 5.section_title: Question Set 5: Vocabulary (Morphology - Root Words and Prefixes)
Year 5.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying root words, (B) Meaning of prefix 'dis-', (C) Meaning of prefix 'mis-'.

subs.q: A Root Word is the most basic part of a word. What is the root word of "disobeying"?
subs.h: Remove the "dis-" from the start and the "-ing" from the end.

subs.q: The Prefix "dis-" usually means "not" or "the opposite of." If "agree" means to think the same, what does "disagree" mean? Options: A) To think the same again, B) To not think the same, C) To think very hard.
subs.h: Use the definition: "dis-" means "not."

subs.q: The prefix "mis-" means "wrongly" or "badly." What does it mean if you "misunderstand" something? Options: A) To understand it well, B) To not understand it at all, C) To understand it the wrong way.
subs.h: Use the definition: "mis-" means "wrongly."

Year 5.mastery_q: If you behave badly or wrongly, which word describes your actions? (Combine the prefix "mis-" with the root word "behave").
Year 5.mastery_hint: Put the prefix meaning "wrongly" at the start of the word "behave."

Year 6.section_title: Question Set 1: Grammar (Active and Passive Voice)
Year 6.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying the subject and object, (B) Recognising the active voice, (C) Recognising the passive voice.

subs.q: In a sentence, the Subject is the person or thing doing the action. In the sentence, "The chef cooked the meal," who is the Subject?
subs.h: Look for who is performing the action of cooking.

subs.q: An Active sentence is when the Subject performs the action. A Passive sentence is when the action happens to the Subject (e.g., The meal was cooked by the chef). Is this sentence Active or Passive: "The window was broken by the ball."? Options: A) Active, B) Passive.
subs.h: Is the window "doing" the breaking, or did the breaking happen "to" the window?

subs.q: To make a sentence passive, we often use the word "by" before the person who did the action. Rewrite this active sentence as a Passive sentence: "The cat chased the mouse."
subs.h: Start your sentence with "The mouse..." and use the word "by."

Year 6.mastery_q: Which of these sentences is written in the Passive Voice? Options: A) The heavy rain flooded the low streets. B) The mistake was corrected by the smart student. C) We ate the delicious cake. D) The dog barked at the stranger.
Year 6.mastery_hint: Look for the sentence where the Subject (the thing at the start) has the action happening to it, usually using "was [action] by..."

Year 6.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying independent clauses, (B) Recognising conjunctions, (C) Using semi-colons to replace conjunctions.

subs.q: An Independent Clause is a group of words that makes sense on its own as a full sentence. Which of these is an Independent Clause? Options: A) Because it was cold, B) The snow fell, C) Under the blue sky.
subs.h: Which one sounds like a complete thought that doesn't need more words?

subs.q: A Conjunction is a joining word like and, but, or so. What is the conjunction in this sentence: "It was raining, so we stayed inside."?
subs.h: It is the small word connecting the two ideas.

subs.q: A Semi-colon (;) can be used to join two independent clauses that are closely related, taking the place of a conjunction. Where should the Semi-colon go to replace the word "but": "I wanted to go; but it was too late."? Options: A) After 'I', B) After 'go', C) After 'late'.
subs.h: Put it exactly where the joining word ("but") was.

Year 6.mastery_q: Use a Semi-colon to join these two sentences into one: "The sun set. The stars appeared."
Year 6.mastery_hint: Write the first sentence, replace the full stop with a semi-colon (;), and then write the second sentence starting with a lowercase letter.

Year 6.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining a Fact, (B) Defining an Opinion, (C) Distinguishing between them in complex text.

subs.q: A Fact is something that can be proven true with evidence or data. Which of these is a Fact? Options: A) Blue is the prettiest color. B) The earth orbits the sun. C) Everyone loves pizza.
subs.h: Which one is true for everyone and can be tested by scientists?

subs.q: An Opinion is a belief, feeling, or view that not everyone agrees with. Which of these is an Opinion? Options: A) A triangle has three sides. B) London is the capital of England. C) This book is the best story ever written.
subs.h: Which one is just how someone "feels" about the book?

subs.q: Words like "think," "believe," "best," or "worst" are clues that a sentence is an Opinion. In the sentence, "I believe the museum is very boring," which word is the clue?
subs.h: It is a word that shows a personal thought.

Year 6.mastery_q: Read this paragraph: "Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. It is located in the Himalayas. Climbing it is the most exciting thing a person can do." Which part of the paragraph is an Opinion? Options: A) Mount Everest is the highest mountain. B) It is located in the Himalayas. C) Climbing it is the most exciting thing.
Year 6.mastery_hint: Two of these can be proven with a map or ruler. One is just how someone feels about climbing.

Year 6.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying synonyms, (B) Using context clues, (C) Selecting precise vocabulary for meaning.

subs.q: A Synonym is a word that has the same or a very similar meaning to another word. What is a synonym for "Happy"? Options: A) Sad, B) Angry, C) Joyful, D) Tired.
subs.h: Which word would you use if you won a prize?

subs.q: Read this: "The abandoned house looked dilapidated; the roof had holes, the windows were smashed, and the door was hanging off its hinges." Based on these clues, does dilapidated mean "new" or "falling apart"?
subs.h: Look at the description: holes in the roof and smashed windows.

subs.q: Which word is more Precise (specific) to describe a very small, light rain? Options: A) Storm, B) Drizzle, C) Downpour.
subs.h: A "downpour" is very heavy. Which one is for light rain?

Year 6.mastery_q: In the following sentence, replace the word "said" with a more precise synonym that shows the character is angry: "Get out of here!" Tom said.
Year 6.mastery_hint: Think of a word that means said in a very loud, cross way (e.g., bellowed, shouted).

Year 6.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying compound adjectives, (B) Understanding "Ambiguity" (unclear meaning), (C) Using hyphens to clarify meaning.

subs.q: A Hyphen (-) is a short dash used to join two words together to make them act like one description. How would you join the words "blue" and "eyed" to describe a "blue eyed boy"?
subs.h: Put the small mark (-) between the two describing words.

subs.q: Ambiguity means a sentence could have two different meanings, which makes it confusing. In the phrase "man eating shark," without a hyphen, does it mean a man is eating a shark, or the shark eats humans? Options: A) Only one meaning, B) Two possible meanings.
subs.h: Could it be a man at a dinner table, or a dangerous animal in the sea?

subs.q: If we add a hyphen to make it "man-eating shark," we are joining "man" and "eating" to describe the shark. Now, what does it mean? Options: A) A man is eating, B) The shark eats people.
subs.h: The hyphen turns "man-eating" into one single description for the shark.

Year 6.mastery_q: Which sentence uses a Hyphen to correctly show that there are thirty animals that are all small? Options: A) There were thirty small-animals. B) There were thirty-small animals.
Year 6.mastery_hint: You want to join the number "thirty" and the size "small" so they both describe the animals together.

Year 7.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining a Metaphor, (B) Identifying a metaphor in a sentence, (C) Identifying the "root" of the comparison.

subs.q: A Metaphor is a type of description that says one thing is another thing to show they share a quality (e.g., "The moon was a silver coin"). What is the word for this type of description?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'M'.

subs.q: In the sentence, "The classroom was a zoo," which word is being used to describe the classroom? Options: A) Was B) Classroom C) Zoo D) The
subs.h: The classroom isn't literally a place for animals, but it shares a quality with one.

subs.q: If a person says, "The snow is a white blanket," what quality does the snow share with a blanket? Options: A) It is cold B) It covers everything C) It is made of wool D) It is falling
subs.h: Think about what a blanket does when you put it over something.

Year 7.mastery_q: Read this sentence: "The golden sun was a heater warming the earth." Identify the word in this metaphor that is used to describe the sun.
Year 7.mastery_hint: The sun is being compared to a specific object that provides heat. Write that object.

Year 7.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying an Independent Clause, (B) Identifying a Subordinating Conjunction, (C) Recognizing a multi-clause sentence.

subs.q: An Independent Clause is a group of words that makes sense as a full sentence on its own. Which of these is an Independent Clause? Options: A) Because it was raining B) The boy ran home C) Although he was tired D) When the sun rose
subs.h: If you said this out loud, which one sounds like a finished thought?

subs.q: A Subordinating Conjunction is a joining word that adds a "maybe" or a "reason" to a sentence, making that part depend on the rest of the sentence. Examples include: because, although, while, if, since. Which of these is a Subordinating Conjunction? Options: A) Dog B) Ran C) Although D) Quickly
subs.h: Look for the word that introduces a condition or reason.

subs.q: In the sentence, "I went to bed because I was tired," the bolded part is a Subordinate Clause. What is the joining word (conjunction) used at the start of that clause?
subs.h: It is the word that explains "why."

Year 7.mastery_q: Which of these is a Complex Sentence (a sentence containing one independent clause and at least one subordinate clause)? Options: A) The cat sat on the mat. B) The cat sat and the dog barked. C) While the cat slept, the dog barked. D) The big cat sat.
Year 7.mastery_hint: Look for the sentence that has a "joining word" like While or Because at the very start.

Year 7.section_title: Question Set 3: Vocabulary & Register (Formal vs. Informal)
Year 7.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying informal language (slang), (B) Identifying formal vocabulary, (C) Selecting language for a specific audience.

subs.q: Informal Language is used with friends (e.g., "Hey, what's up?"). Formal Language is used for serious writing or with people in authority (e.g., "Good morning, how are you?"). Which of these is Informal? Options: A) I require assistance. B) Give us a hand, mate. C) Please may you help me? D) I would like some help.
subs.h: Look for words you would only say to a close friend.

subs.q: In formal writing, we avoid "slang." What is a more Formal word for the slang word "telly"?
subs.h: It is the full name of the machine you watch shows on.

subs.q: Which word is the most Formal way to say you are "sorry"? Options: A) My bad B) Sorry C) Apologise D) Whoops
subs.h: This word is often used in official letters or by a principal.

Year 7.mastery_q: You are writing a letter to a local Member of Parliament. Which word should you use to describe a problem: "issue" or "hassle"?
Year 7.mastery_hint: Choose the word that sounds professional and serious (Standard English).

Year 7.section_title: Question Set 4: Punctuation (The Colon for Lists)
Year 7.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying an Independent Clause, (B) Knowing the symbol for a Colon, (C) Using a colon to introduce a list.

subs.q: A Colon is a punctuation mark that consists of two dots, one above the other. Which of these is a Colon? Options: A) ; B) : C) , D) .
subs.h: It looks like the symbol used between hours and minutes on a digital clock (12:00).

subs.q: A colon can be used to introduce a list. However, the words before the colon must make sense as a full sentence. Which of these can have a colon added after it? Options: A) I bought B) At the shop I bought C) I bought three items D) Because I bought
subs.h: Which one is an Independent Clause (a full thought) on its own?

subs.q: Where should the colon go in this sentence: "You will need these tools a hammer, a nail, and a saw."?
subs.h: Put it right after the word "tools."

Year 7.mastery_q: Rewrite this sentence with the Colon in the correct place to introduce the list: "The cake requires four ingredients flour, eggs, sugar, and butter."
Year 7.mastery_hint: Look for the full thought that ends just before the list starts. Put the (:) there.

Year 7.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Literal fact retrieval, (B) Identifying character emotion, (C) Making an inference (reading between the lines).

subs.q: Read this: "Arthur stared at the giant pile of dirty dishes. He sighed deeply, rolled up his sleeves, and turned on the hot water tap." What is Arthur looking at?
subs.h: Look at the very first sentence.

subs.q: A Sigh is a long breath out that usually shows someone is tired or frustrated. Based on Arthur's "deep sigh," how is he likely feeling about the dishes? Options: A) Excited B) Unhappy/Reluctant C) Happy D) Scared
subs.h: Does he want to do the dishes, or does he think it is a big, boring job?

subs.q: An Inference is using clues to understand something not explicitly stated. If Arthur "rolled up his sleeves" and "turned on the tap," what is he about to do? Options: A) Go for a swim B) Wash the dishes C) Cook a meal D) Take a nap
subs.h: People roll up their sleeves to keep them dry while they work with water.

Year 7.mastery_q: Read this: "The sky turned a bruised purple, and the birds suddenly went silent. In the distance, a low rumble echoed through the valley." What is about to happen? Options: A) A sunset B) A birthday party C) A storm D) A parade
Year 7.mastery_hint: Think about what "bruised purple" clouds and a "low rumble" (thunder) usually mean.

Year 8.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining Personification, (B) Identifying human actions in non-human objects, (C) Identifying the object being described.

subs.q: Personification is a type of description where a non-human object (like a tree or a car) is given human qualities or feelings. What is the name of this device?
subs.h: It starts with the word "Person."

subs.q: In the sentence, "The wind whistled through the trees," which word describes an action that a human usually does?
subs.h: Humans do this with their lips to make a high-pitched sound.

subs.q: If a writer says, "The sun crawled across the sky," which non-human object is being given a human action?
subs.h: What is the "Who" or the "Thing" moving in the sky?

Year 8.mastery_q: Identify the Personification used in this sentence: "The old, stubborn car refused to start in the cold morning."
Year 8.mastery_hint: Look for the word that describes a human character trait (like being difficult or set in your ways) applied to the car.

Year 8.section_title: Question Set 2: Punctuation (The Dash for Emphasis)
Year 8.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Parenthesis, (B) Knowing the symbol for a Dash, (C) Using a dash to add emphasis.

subs.q: Parenthesis is extra information added into a sentence (like this). If you take it out, the sentence still makes sense. What is the name for this "extra information"?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'P'.

subs.q: A Dash is a horizontal line ( — ) used to mark a break in a sentence. It is longer than a hyphen. What is this punctuation mark called?
subs.h: It rhymes with "bash" or "crash."

subs.q: A dash can be used to add extra information at the end of a sentence for emphasis (to make it stand out). In the sentence: "He reached the summit — exhausted," which word is being emphasized?
subs.h: Look at the word after the dash.

Year 8.mastery_q: Read this sentence: "The explorer finally found the ancient treasure — a single gold coin." What is the specific Parenthesis (the extra information) added for emphasis in this sentence?
Year 8.mastery_hint: Write the words that come after the dash.

Year 8.section_title: Question Set 3: Grammar (Active and Passive Voice)
Year 8.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying the Subject (the doer), (B) Identifying the Object (the receiver), (C) Distinguishing voice.

subs.q: The Subject of a sentence is the person or thing performing the action. In the sentence: "The firefighter saved the cat," who is the Subject?
subs.h: Who did the "saving"?

subs.q: The Object of a sentence is the person or thing that has the action done to it. In the same sentence ("The firefighter saved the cat"), what is the Object?
subs.h: Who was the action of saving done to?

subs.q: A Passive sentence is when the Object is moved to the start of the sentence (e.g., "The cat was saved by the firefighter"). Which word is usually used before the person who did the action in a passive sentence?
subs.h: It is a small two-letter word: "It was done ___ me."

Year 8.mastery_q: Is the following sentence written in the Active voice or the Passive voice? "The delicious meal was prepared by the talented chef."
Year 8.mastery_hint: Look at the start of the sentence. Is the "Meal" doing the preparing, or is the preparing happening to the meal?

Year 8.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying questions, (B) Defining Persuasion, (C) Understanding the purpose of a rhetorical question.

subs.q: A sentence that asks for information and ends with a "?" is called a __________.
subs.h: It is the opposite of an answer.

subs.q: Persuasion is when you try to convince someone to agree with your point of view. What is the word for "trying to convince someone"?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'P'.

subs.q: A Rhetorical Question is a question used in a speech that does not need an answer. It is used to make the audience think. What is this type of question called?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'R'.

Year 8.mastery_q: Read this line from a speech about the environment: "Do you really want our beautiful oceans to be filled with plastic?" What is the name of this specific persuasive device?
Year 8.mastery_hint: It is a question that the speaker expects the audience to think about, but not answer out loud.

Year 8.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Adjectives, (B) Defining Tone, (C) Linking vocabulary to atmosphere.

subs.q: An Adjective is a describing word. In the phrase "the gloomy cave," which word is the Adjective?
subs.h: Which word tells you what the cave is like?

subs.q: Tone is the "mood" or "attitude" of a piece of writing (e.g., happy, scary, serious). What is the word for the "attitude" of the author?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'T'.

subs.q: If a story uses words like "dark," "silent," "shadow," and "shivering," is the Tone likely to be Cheerful or Ominous (scary)?
subs.h: Think about a horror movie.

Year 8.mastery_q: Read this passage: "The sun burst through the clouds, and the children laughed as they ran through the bright, colorful fields." What is the Tone of this passage?
Year 8.mastery_hint: Use an adjective that describes a happy and positive feeling.

Year 9.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Anaphora, (B) Identifying Tricolons, (C) Identifying Antithesis.

subs.q: Anaphora is when a word or phrase is repeated at the start of several sentences in a row to build excitement (e.g., "We shall fight... We shall win"). Which of these is an example of Anaphora? Options: A) He ran, he jumped, he fell. B) Love is kind; love is blind. C) The sky is blue and the grass is green.
subs.h: Look for the sentence where the same words are repeated at the very beginning of each part.

subs.q: A Tricolon is a list of three related ideas or words used to make a point more memorable (e.g., "Eat, sleep, repeat"). How many items must be in a list for it to be a Tricolon?
subs.h: The prefix "tri-" means the same as in "triangle."

subs.q: Antithesis is when a writer puts two completely opposite ideas together in one sentence to show a contrast (e.g., "Search for peace, prepare for war"). Which of these is an Antithesis? Options: A) It was a cold, dark night. B) One small step for man, one giant leap for mankind. C) The cat sat on the mat.
subs.h: Look for the sentence that contrasts "small" with "giant."

Year 9.mastery_q: Read this line from a speech: "We must find the light. We must fight the dark. We must use our hearts, our hands, and our heads to win."
Year 9.mastery_hint: The Anaphora is the phrase repeated at the start; the Tricolon is the list of three things at the end.

Year 9.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Iambic Pentameter, (B) Defining Hamartia (Fatal Flaw), (C) Defining Hubris.

subs.q: Iambic Pentameter is a rhythm in poetry that sounds like a heartbeat (da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM, da-DUM). It has exactly 10 syllables per line. Which of these lines is in Iambic Pentameter? Options: A) To be or not to be, that is the question. B) But soft, what light through yonder window breaks? C) The cat sat.
subs.h: Clap the beats. Line B has exactly 10 syllables.

subs.q: Hamartia is a "fatal flaw"—a character's specific weakness (like jealousy or greed) that leads to their death. If a hero dies because he is too ambitious, what is his Hamartia?
subs.h: The answer is the personality trait that caused the problem.

subs.q: Hubris is a specific type of Hamartia. it means "excessive pride" or thinking you are better than the gods or the law. What is the English word for Hubris?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'P'.

Year 9.mastery_q: A hero believes he is more powerful than Fate and ignores all warnings, leading to his downfall. Is this an example of Hubris or Iambic Pentameter?
Year 9.mastery_hint: Does this describe a "rhythm of words" or a "character's excessive pride"?

Year 9.section_title: Question Set 3: Writing (Advanced Pacing and Punctuation)
Year 9.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Using Ellipsis for suspense, (B) Identifying Independent Clauses, (C) Using Semicolons to join clauses.

subs.q: An Ellipsis is a set of three dots (...). It is used to show a pause or to create suspense. What is the name of this punctuation mark: ...?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'E'.

subs.q: An Independent Clause is a group of words that makes sense as a full sentence on its own. Is "The door opened" an independent clause?
subs.h: If you said this to a friend, would they understand the whole thought?

subs.q: A Semicolon (;) is used to join two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning. Which is correct? Options: A) It was dark; I was scared. B) It was dark; because I was scared.
subs.h: Both sides of the (;) must be able to stand as full sentences. "Because I was scared" is not a full sentence.

Year 9.mastery_q: Rewrite these two sentences as one sentence using a Semicolon for cohesion and an Ellipsis to create a dramatic pause at the end: "The hunter waited. Something moved in the shadows."
Year 9.mastery_hint: Join the two sentences with a (;) and put the (...) after the very last word.

Year 9.section_title: Question Set 4: Reading Language (19th Century Context)
Year 9.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining the "Industrial Revolution," (B) Identifying "Societal Anxiety," (C) Analyzing Authorial Perspective.

subs.q: The Industrial Revolution was a time (1800s) when people moved from farms to cities to work in noisy, smoky factories. Which word describes this time? Options: A) Romantic B) Industrial C) Medieval
subs.h: Think about factories and industry.

subs.q: Societal Anxiety is a fancy term for when a large group of people are "worried" about something new (like new science or machines). What does "Anxiety" mean?
subs.h: It is a feeling of being very worried or nervous.

subs.q: Authorial Perspective is the author's point of view. If an author describes a factory as a "dark, hungry monster," do they have a Positive or Negative perspective on factories?
subs.h: Is a "monster" a good thing or a bad thing?

Year 9.mastery_q: In a 19th-century novel, a scientist creates a life-form that he cannot control. This reflects a Societal Anxiety about science going too far. What is the Authorial Perspective on new science in this story?
Year 9.mastery_hint: Does the author think science is "safe" or "dangerous" if it leads to a monster that can't be controlled?

Year 9.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying a "Linear" story, (B) Defining a "Circular Narrative," (C) Identifying a "Flash-forward."

subs.q: A Linear story moves in a straight line from start to finish. A Circular Narrative is a story that ends in the same place it began. If a story starts at a park and ends at the exact same park, what is its structure? Options: A) Linear B) Circular
subs.h: Think of a circle. You end up where you started.

subs.q: A Flash-forward is a structural device where the story suddenly jumps into the future to show what will happen later. What is the name for "jumping into the future"?
subs.h: It is the opposite of a "Flashback."

subs.q: Pacing is the speed at which a story is told. To make a scene feel fast and urgent, should a writer use very long sentences or very short sentences?
subs.h: Think about breathing. Short sentences make you read faster.

Year 9.mastery_q: A writer wants to show a character's life is a "never-ending trap." Which Structural Device would best show that the character's journey always ends up back at the start? Options: A) Flash-forward B) Circular Narrative C) Linear Chronology
Year 9.mastery_hint: Look for the word that means the story goes in a "circle."

Year 10.section_title: Question Set 1: Persuasive Spoken English (Anaphora and Tricolon)
Year 10.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying repeated beginnings (Anaphora), (B) Identifying lists of three (Tricolon), (C) Differentiating formal Standard English.

subs.q: Anaphora is when a word or phrase is repeated at the start of following sentences to create a rhythm (e.g., "I have a dream... I have a dream..."). In the speech: "We will fight. We will win," what is the Anaphora?
subs.h: Which two words start both sentences?

subs.q: A Tricolon is a list of three related words or phrases used for impact (e.g., "Friends, Romans, Countrymen"). Which of these is a Tricolon? Options: A) Stop and look. B) Stop, look, and listen.
subs.h: Count how many actions are in the list.

subs.q: Standard English is formal language that avoids slang (like "gonna"). Which word is Standard English: "require" or "want"?
subs.h: Which word sounds more professional in a business letter?

Year 10.mastery_q: Identify the Tricolon used in this formal speech: "We must act with courage. We must act with speed. We must act for our homes, our children, and our future."
Year 10.mastery_hint: Look at the very last sentence. Provide the three specific things we must act for.

Year 10.section_title: Question Set 2: Shakespearean Tragedy (Soliloquy and Hamartia)
Year 10.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying a character alone (Soliloquy), (B) Defining a character flaw (Hamartia), (C) Identifying the "Subject" of a sentence.

subs.q: A Soliloquy is when a character in a play speaks their thoughts out loud to the audience while they are alone on stage. What is the name of this device?
subs.h: It starts with "Soli-".

subs.q: Hamartia is a "fatal flaw" or a specific mistake in a hero's character (like being too proud) that leads to their downfall. If a hero falls because of their jealousy, what is their Hamartia?
subs.h: Identify the negative emotion mentioned.

subs.q: In a sentence, the Subject is the person doing the action. In the sentence: "The king wept alone," who is the Subject?
subs.h: Who is doing the action of weeping?

Year 10.mastery_q: A character stands alone on stage and says, "My own ambition will be my end." What is the Subject of this sentence, and what is the character's Hamartia?
Year 10.mastery_hint: The Subject is the "Who/What" that will be the "end." The Hamartia is the specific flaw the character names.

Year 10.section_title: Question Set 3: Reading Analysis (Fact vs. Bias)
Year 10.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Distinguishing facts, (B) Identifying subjective adjectives (Opinion), (C) Defining Bias.

subs.q: A Fact is information that can be proven true (e.g., "The sun is hot"). Which is a Fact? Options: A) Coffee is tasty. B) Coffee contains caffeine.
subs.h: Which one can be tested in a lab?

subs.q: An Opinion uses "Subjective" words that show a person's feelings. Which word in this sentence is Subjective: "The rude waiter served the food"?
subs.h: Which word tells you how the writer felt about the waiter?

subs.q: Bias is an unfair preference for one side. If a newspaper only interviews people who like a new law and ignores people who hate it, is that Bias?
subs.h: Is the reporting balanced or one-sided?

Year 10.mastery_q: Read this sentence: "The brilliant mayor easily defeated the weak opponent." Identify the two subjective words that show the writer has a Bias toward the mayor.
Year 10.mastery_hint: Look for the two describing words (adjectives) that show the mayor is "good" and the opponent is "bad."

Year 10.section_title: Question Set 4: Syntactic Precision (Semicolons and Clauses)
Year 10.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying an Independent Clause, (B) Identifying a semicolon, (C) Joining clauses for cohesion.

subs.q: An Independent Clause is a group of words that can stand alone as a full sentence. Is "The dog barked" an independent clause?
subs.h: If you said this to a friend, would it sound like a finished thought?

subs.q: A Semicolon is a mark (;) used to join two independent clauses that are closely related. What is the name of this mark?
subs.h: It looks like a dot over a comma.

subs.q: A semicolon can replace a full stop. Which is correct? Options: A) I am cold; I forgot my coat. B) I am cold; because I forgot my coat.
subs.h: Remember, both sides of the (;) must be full sentences on their own.

Year 10.mastery_q: Use a Semicolon to join these two ideas into one sentence: "The clock struck midnight. The lights went out."
Year 10.mastery_hint: Write the first sentence, put the (;), and then write the second sentence starting with a lowercase 't'.

Year 10.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining Verbal Irony, (B) Identifying Situational Irony, (C) Defining Dramatic Irony.

subs.q: Verbal Irony is when someone says the opposite of what they mean (e.g., saying "What a great day" during a storm). Is this Irony?
subs.h: Is the speaker being literal or the opposite?

subs.q: Situational Irony is when the outcome is the opposite of what was expected (e.g., a fire station burning down). If a police station is robbed, is that ironic?
subs.h: Do you expect a police station to be the safest place or the easiest to rob?

subs.q: Dramatic Irony is when the audience knows a secret that a character in the book does not know. What is the name of this device?
subs.h: It starts with the letter 'D'.

Year 10.mastery_q: In a story, a thief sneaks into a house to steal a safe. The audience has already seen the owners empty the safe earlier that morning, but the thief doesn't know. What specific type of Irony is this?
Year 10.mastery_hint: Does the audience know more than the character? Check the definition in Sub-Question 3.

Year 11.section_title: Question Set 1: Spoken English (Critiquing Arguments & Rebuttal)
Year 11.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying a core argument, (B) Defining and identifying evidence, (C) Formulating a rebuttal.

subs.q: An Argument is a statement put forward to persuade others that an action or idea is right or wrong. Read this statement: "Schools should start at 10:00 AM because teenagers' brains function better later in the day." What is the core argument being made here?
subs.h: Look for the main change being suggested.

subs.q: Evidence is a set of facts or data used to support an argument. In the statement above, what specific reason is given as evidence?
subs.h: Look for the words following "because."

subs.q: A Rebuttal is a counter-argument used to show that someone else's argument is weak or wrong. If someone argues that a 10:00 AM start is good for brains, which of these is a Rebuttal based on a "practical" problem? Options: A) Teenagers like to sleep. B) Teachers would also be more awake. C) It would be difficult for parents to drop children off before they go to work.
subs.h: Look for the option that presents a new problem or "downside."

Year 11.mastery_q: You are part of an academic panel. A peer argues: "Social media is entirely negative because it reduces face-to-face talk." Provide a Rebuttal that offers a synthesis (a combination) of a different viewpoint.
Year 11.mastery_hint: A good rebuttal often starts with: "While I agree that it can reduce talking in person, it also allows people to..." (Finish the thought with a positive).

Year 11.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining Soliloquy, (B) Identifying Hamartia (Fatal Flaw), (C) Analyzing Dramatic Irony.

subs.q: A Soliloquy is a dramatic device where a character speaks their private thoughts out loud while alone on stage. What is the name for a "long speech made alone to the audience"?
subs.h: It starts with "Soli-".

subs.q: Hamartia is a technical term for a "fatal flaw"—a specific personality weakness (like pride or jealousy) that leads to a hero’s downfall. If a king's downfall is caused because he is too proud to listen to advice, what is his Hamartia?
subs.h: Identify the personality weakness mentioned.

subs.q: Dramatic Irony occurs when the audience knows a secret that the characters on stage do not know. If the audience knows a letter is a fake, but the hero believes it is real and acts on it, is this Dramatic Irony?
subs.h: Does the audience have more information than the character?

Year 11.mastery_q: Read this summary: "In a soliloquy, the hero reveals his plan to kill the King, unaware that the King's guards are hiding behind a curtain listening." Is the hero's lack of awareness an example of Dramatic Irony or Hamartia?
Year 11.mastery_hint: Is the situation caused by the audience/guards knowing something the hero doesn't, or is it caused by a character flaw?

Year 11.section_title: Question Set 3: Reading Language (Poetic & Language Devices)
Year 11.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining Sibilance, (B) Defining Oxymoron, (C) Analyzing Pathetic Fallacy.

subs.q: Sibilance is a type of alliteration where "s" or "sh" sounds are repeated to create a hissing or soft sound. Which of these uses Sibilance? Options: A) Big blue boat B) Seven slippery snakes C) Hot heavy hills.
subs.h: Listen for the "s" sounds.

subs.q: An Oxymoron is a figure of speech where two opposite words are put together (e.g., "bittersweet" or "loud silence"). What is the Oxymoron in the phrase "The deafening silence of the empty house"?
subs.h: Find the two words that have opposite meanings.

subs.q: Pathetic Fallacy is when a writer gives human emotions to the weather to reflect the mood of the story (e.g., it rains when a character is sad). If a character is angry and a violent thunderstorm begins, is this Pathetic Fallacy?
subs.h: Does the weather match the character's mood?

Year 11.mastery_q: Read this sentence: "The cruel wind hissed through the trees as the giant midget stepped forward." Which two devices are used here?
Year 11.mastery_hint: Look for a human emotion given to the wind (Sub 3 logic) and two opposite words put together (Sub 2 logic).

Year 11.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Defining Anaphora, (B) Defining Tricolon, (C) Identifying the "Register."

subs.q: Anaphora is the repetition of a word or phrase at the beginning of nearby sentences to add emphasis. In the speech: "We shall fight. We shall win. We shall survive," what is the Anaphora?
subs.h: Which two words are repeated at the start of every sentence?

subs.q: A Tricolon (or Rule of Three) is when a writer lists three related words or phrases to make an idea more memorable. Which of these is a Tricolon? Options: A) Blood and sweat B) Blood, sweat, and tears C) Blood.
subs.h: Count how many items are in the list.

subs.q: Register refers to the level of formality. A Formal Register avoids slang and contractions (like "can't"). Which sentence is in a Formal Register? Options: A) It's gonna be great. B) This will be an excellent opportunity.
subs.h: Which one sounds like a professional speech?

Year 11.mastery_q: You are writing a persuasive speech for an exam. You want to use Anaphora and a Tricolon in a Formal Register. Which of these is the best opening? Options: A) We need help. We need food. We need water. B) It's bad, it's sad, and it's mad. C) We must act now. We must act together. We must act for our future, our families, and our freedom.
Year 11.mastery_hint: Look for the sentence that repeats the start ("We must act") AND has a list of three things at the end.

Year 11.instruction: Tutor: Skill Mapping: (A) Identifying Independent Clauses, (B) Using a Semicolon for cohesion, (C) Identifying Ambiguity.

subs.q: An Independent Clause is a group of words that can stand alone as a full sentence. Is "The rain stopped" an independent clause?
subs.h: Does it make sense as a complete thought?

subs.q: A Semicolon (;) is used to join two independent clauses that are closely related in meaning. Where should the semicolon go: "The sun set the moon rose."?
subs.h: Put it where the first full sentence ends.

subs.q: Ambiguity occurs when a sentence has more than one possible meaning, which can be confusing. In the sentence "I saw a man with a telescope," does it mean the man had a telescope, or you used a telescope to see him?
subs.h: Could both meanings be true based only on those words?

Year 11.mastery_q: Look at this sentence: "The students finished the exam; they were exhausted." Does the Semicolon correctly join two Independent Clauses? (Answer "Yes" or "No").
Year 11.mastery_hint: Check if "The students finished the exam" can be a sentence AND if "they were exhausted" can be a sentence.
